entries.title: Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
entries.summary: Spain's cabinet ministers said they have consensus on new measures to curb the housing crisis in the country after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen last week from her apartment sparked protests.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction

September 29, 2026

Spain's cabinet ministers said they have consensus on new measures to curb the housing crisis in the country after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen last week from her apartment sparked protests.

Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.

Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.

"It's ‌time ​to intervene in the speculative housing market and ​begin to rebalance the scales between ⁠citizens ​and vulture funds," ​Garcia, who belongs ​to the ‌leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, ​wrote ⁠in a post on ⁠X.

Legislation still needs to pass through parliament

The Spanish government, led byPrime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.

But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.

Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.

Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.

What's the Maricarmen case that sparked protests in Spain?

Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.

Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.

Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.

According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.

The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.

Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.

She is a wheelchair user too.

People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.

More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.

Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says

Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."

"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.

"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Albania: As corruption cases multiply, experts question whether the anti-corruption drive is addressing the causes or just the symptoms
entries.summary: From a former president to the ex-intelligence chief, Albania is prosecuting senior officials at a rate once thought impossible. But do more prosecutions mean less corruption or simply better enforcement?
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

From a former president to the ex-intelligence chief, Albania is prosecuting senior officials at a rate once thought impossible. But do more prosecutions mean less corruption or simply better enforcement?

On September 22, the head of Albania's State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni, was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service chiefs. Back in Tirana, the Special Court had ordered her house arrest over two suspected criminal offences: supporting the perpetrator of a crime and disclosure of investigative secrecy.

The investigation into Hyseni emerged from a wider corruption case involving the National Agency for Information Society (AKSHI), the agency responsible for much of Albania's digital public infrastructure.

Prosecutors suspect that she used information available to her as intelligence chief to help a person wanted in that investigation.

Hyseni turned herself in to the Albanian authorities later that day and remains under house arrest as the investigation continues. She has since been dismissed as head of the intelligence service.

Rise in criminal proceedings and investigations

Hyseni's case is the latest in a series of criminal proceedings that have reached unusually high into Albania's political and state establishment.

A former president has spent almost two years in detention, a former prime minister is on trial, the mayor of Tirana has been behind bars since early 2025, two former deputy prime ministers under Prime Minister Edi Rama have also faced criminal proceedings, and investigations have been launched into senior officials in agencies controlling large areas of public spending and state infrastructure.

These are all separate cases, but they all involve alleged abuse of public power.

How did Albania get here?

For years, the problem was completely the opposite: High-level corruption in Albania was widely associated with impunity.

This is why bringing senior political figures accused of wrongdoing before the courts became one of the central expectations of the justice reform launched in 2016.

"The expectation was that the new justice institutions would focus on high-level corruption and 'VIP' cases," says Afrim Krasniqi, a political scientist and executive director of the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. "There were individuals who stood above the law, and impunity was pronounced," he told DW.

The reform fundamentally reshaped Albania's justice system and created new institutions to investigate corruption and organized crime, including the Special Anti-Corruption Structure, SPAK.

But the change was not immediate. Building the new institutions took years, and older cases were often more difficult to investigate.

For Dorian Matlija, a lawyer and executive director of Albanian civil society organization Res Publica, the number of senior officials now facing criminal proceedings does not necessarily mean that corruption is more widespread today than it was in the past.

"What has changed significantly is the institutional reaction," Matlija told DW. "Today, SPAK is a specialized structure with greater independence, stronger capacities and international support, as well as the willingness to undertake investigations that have broken the myth of the untouchability of senior officials."

The other side of accountability

But bringing senior officials before the courts is only one measure of whether institutions are working.

By the time a corruption case reaches prosecutors, the alleged abuse has already taken place. For Matlija, this is where Albania's progress is far less clear.

"We are becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it," he said.

Matlija points to the institutions and mechanisms that are supposed to act before a case becomes criminal: administrative controls, audits, conflict-of-interest rules and asset declarations. In his assessment, these have often proved ineffective.

The European Commission's 2025 report on Albania reaches a similar conclusion. It said that SPAK has made "tangible progress towards a solid track record in the fight against corruption." At the same time, the report says that corruption remains widespread and that "the institutional framework for prevention of corruption continued to have a limited impact."

The impact on citizens

The problem is also visible in citizens' encounters with public officials.

In a 2023 survey by the anti-corruption and good governance coalition SELDI (Southeast Europe Leadership for Development and Integrity), 52% of respondents in Albania said they had experienced corruption pressure from public officials, while 40% reported having paid a bribe.

Krasniqi sees the problem in broader political terms. Albania has been governed by Rama's Socialist Party since 2013, and the party currently holds an outright majority in parliament. He argues that this prolonged political dominance has weakened the checks and balances that should constrain the executive.

"We have a deformed system," he said. "The head of the executive controls the executive, parliament and institutions."

He argues that this concentration of power has been accompanied by informal networks of influence, with people outside state institutions able to shape political decisions, legislation and the use of public assets.

Rama has repeatedly maintained that criminal responsibility is individual when investigations have reached senior officials. Responding to the Hyseni case, he returned to the same position.

"When a senior official has opened an account with justice, the case of the former intelligence chief is an individual matter between her and the justice system," Rama said.

What does this mean for Albania's EU accession hopes?

In May, the EU confirmed that the country had met the interim benchmarks for the "fundamentals" cluster, which includes the rule of law, and moved into a phase focused on implementation and lasting results.

Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index shows Albania improving from 33 points in 2012 to 39 in 2025 but still ranking below all EU member states.

For Matlija, Albania's efforts to advance EU integration helped create the conditions that allowed institutions such as SPAK to become stronger and more independent.

"The EU no longer demands only the adoption of laws and reforms, but also concrete and sustainable results. This creates constant pressure for justice institutions to be genuinely effective and independent of political power," he said.

For Krasniqi, this is also where the meaning of European integration lies. Membership, he argues, should not be judged only by Albania's progress through the formal accession process, but by whether the country itself changes.

"The essence should be for Albania, Albanian society and Albanian institutions to change and improve, so that we become worthy of integration," he said. For him, that change should also be felt by citizens through greater social security, prosperity and independence, rather than being just a series of formal achievements.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Israel bans Arab parties from election: What you need to know
entries.summary: Israel's push to ban Arab parties from standing in the upcoming election has been called "another nail in the coffin of democracy." Is there a legal basis for doing this, and what could it mean for Arab voters?
entries.content:
Israel

Why and how is Israel banning Arab parties from election?

September 29, 2026

Israel's push to ban Arab parties from standing in the upcoming election has been called "another nail in the coffin of democracy." Is there a legal basis for doing this, and what could it mean for Arab voters?

With less than a month until the Israeli elections, a move from the country's Central Elections Committee (CEC) to bar all Arab parties from running has ignited a debate about the relationship between security, national identity and democratic representation in Israel.

Should the bans remain in place when Israel goes to the polls on October 27, Arab citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country's population, will find themselves without their most likely source of representation in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.

However, the decision is not final, and the Supreme Court could overrule it in the coming days.

Which Arab parties have been banned from the election?

Perhaps the most high-profile party to be banned is Ra'am, otherwise known as The United Arab List. The party currently holds five of the 120 seats in the Knesset and takes a conservative, Islamic position. Earlier this year it announced that it would allow Jewish candidates to stand for the party, with former Israeli police commissioner and deputy minister of national security, Yoav Segalovitz, set to run if the party is permitted.

The ban also applies to The Joint List, a coalition of three parties — Hadash (a left-wing Jewish-Arab party), Ta'al (an Arab nationalist party) and Balad (a Palestinian nationalist party).

The alliance was formed in part to avoid splitting votes and to ensure the parties clear Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. Together, Hadash and Ta'al currently hold five Knesset seats, while Balad has no representation in the outgoing parliament. In recent polls, the parties jointly hold at least seven seats.

The CEC also banned two individual candidates from the joint list. These were the chairman of Balad, Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian-Israeli politician and former member of the Knesset (MK), and Ofer Cassif, a Jewish lawmaker and current MK for Hadash.

The CEC comprises representatives from the outgoing parliament, meaning Likud is well represented. It reportedly voted 18-5 to bar Ra'am and the Joint List on Wednesday. The following day, the committee rejected a petition against National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party. Ben-Gvir recently drew criticism from Germany and many other countries for saying that he thinks "targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza" regardless of whether those people posed an immediate threat.

While a representative of the Supreme Court chairs the Central Elections Committee, the court will ultimately decide the ban after the Adalah rights group confirmed it would appeal on behalf of the parties.

Why are these parties banned?

Right-wing parties such as Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Otzma Yehudit started petitions to ban these parties and individuals. A stipulation in the Knesset's basic law bans candidates who show "negation of the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state," "incitement to racism" or "support for armed struggle by a hostile state or a terrorist organization against the State of Israel."

Supporters of the bans argued that some of the parties' leaders had made statements or engaged in conduct that crossed those legal boundaries. In Ra'am's case, petitioners cited alleged connections between organizations linked to the party and bodies connected to Hamas, as well as statements by Mansour Abbas that they claimed reflected contradictory messages to Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking audiences.

Petitions against Sami Abu Shehadeh and Ofer Cassif similarly relied on past statements and writings that opponents argued amounted to support for positions that undermine the existence of Israel as a Jewish state.

What is the response of those banned?

Ra'am and the Joint List strongly reject the allegations.

Ra'am argues that petitioners failed to provide the clear and convincing evidence required under Israeli law. The party points to Mansour Abbas' condemnation of the October 7 attacks and his efforts on behalf of Israeli hostages as evidence that it does not support terrorism.

The rights organization Adalah, which is representing the parties, said "the CEC conducted an illegitimate political process aimed at persecuting ideas the majority does not accept, and it ended with the disqualification of all Palestinian representation in the Israeli Knesset."

The Joint List said the move amounted to an attempt to disenfranchise more than a million Arab citizens and accused the government of seeking to suppress Arab political participation.

Cassif struck a similar tone on X, when he called the decision "another nail in the coffin of the remnants of democracy" in Israel.

Has this happened before?

Not on this scale. While Israel's election authorities have previously attempted to disqualify Arab parties and candidates, the exclusion of all major Arab-led electoral lists at the same time would be unprecedented.

Balad, in particular, has been previously banned, before a Supreme Court ruling allowed the party to run after all. This happened in 2022, 2019, 2009 and 2003, often unanimously. Cassif's ban in 2019 was also overturned.

Since a 1985 legal amendment allowed such challenges from the committee, the Supreme Court has upheld only one such decision — against the ultra-nationalist Orthodox Jewish party Kach in 1988.

What has the reaction been to the banning of Arab parties from the Israeli election?

Many supporters of the bans argue that the October 7 attack and subsequent war in Gaza changed the political context.

They contend that statements or activities that may previously have been tolerated should be viewed more seriously after the Hamas-led attack and during an ongoing regional conflict.

Ahead of the CEC decision, Netanyahu's Likud party spelled out its backing for a ban. "There is no room in the Knesset for those who harm IDF soldiers and are unable to say that Hamas and Hezbollah are terrorist organizations," said a party statement.

Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza following October 7, 2023.

Responses from the Israeli center, meanwhile, have been divided.

Some centrist politicians have supported disqualifying specific candidates, while expressing concerns over excluding entire party lists representing a substantial minority of Israeli citizens.

Perhaps crucially, Israel's legal establishment has so far not endorsed the disqualifications. The office of Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara reportedly concluded that the evidence against Ra'am and the Joint List did not satisfy the legal requirements for exclusion, although it did support the ban of Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh.

Much of the media reaction has been scathing, with an opinion piece in the Jerusalem Post reading: "Israel has spent decades proudly calling itself the only democracy in the Middle East. Attempting to exclude the political representatives of Arab citizens, who make up roughly a fifth of Israeli society, is dangerous and fundamentally undemocratic."

Meanwhile, the Times of Israel lamented the CEC's back-and-forth banning process, saying that it's a "safe bet that on October 27, voters will be able to cast ballots for the Joint List and Ra'am," before adding that: "Given the unsuccessful track record of these disqualifications, coalition politicians may have been willing to play fast and lose with democratic rights in order to throw some red meat to their base and delegitimize the Arab parties — all while counting on the Supreme Court to maintain the status quo."

entries.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy products and motorcycles takes effect as trade dispute escalates
entries.summary: Donald Trump's ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian goods has come into force, further escalating a trade dispute between the longtime allies.
entries.content:
United States of America

US ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy, motorcycles takes effect

September 29, 2026

Donald Trump's ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian goods has come into force, further escalating a trade dispute between the longtime allies.

The United States on Tuesday began banning imports of a range of Canadian products, including alcoholic beverages, some dairy products and motorcycles.

The move marks the latest escalation in the trade dispute between the two neighboring countries.

What Canadian products has the US banned?

The measures took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT (04:01 GMT/UTC) and replace 50% tariffs that the US had imposed on some of the products since August.

The ban covers nearly $1 billion (€850 million) in annual Canadian imports, although that represents only a small fraction of the roughly $880 billion in goods traded between the two countries each year.

Affected products include alcoholic drinks such as beer, wine, whisky, vodka and rum, as well as non-alcoholic beer, molasses and some dairy products, including whey and protein concentrates.

The ban also covers Canadian-made motorcycles and mopeds with combustion engines larger than 800 cubic centimeters (49 cubic inches).

Why has Trump imposed the ban?

US President Donald Trump's administration says Canada discriminates against American dairy, vehicle and alcohol exporters.

The latest measures follow a series of retaliatory moves between the two countries.

Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of Canadian imports over the summer. Canada responded with tariffs of between 15% and 50% on an equivalent value of US goods.

Some Canadian provinces also removed US alcoholic beverages from store shelves.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the bans were a consequence of Canada's treatment of American exports.

How significant is the economic impact?

Jacob Jensen of the American Action Forum estimated that the ban covers $967 million in Canadian imports based on 2025 figures, with alcoholic beverages accounting for 87% of the total.

The previous 50% tariffs had already made importing many of the affected products uneconomical.

However, analysts warned that the move could provoke further Canadian retaliation and complicate efforts to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

entries.title: Iraq: US troops withdraw from their Iraqi US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against ISIS after 12 years as Baghdad delays militia disarmament
entries.summary: As the US completes its military withdrawal from Iraq, Baghdad declares a new era of sovereignty. But as US troops leave, questions remain over militias, foreign forces and the country's future security.
entries.content:
Iraq

Iraq: US withdrawal leaves security questions

September 29, 2026

As the US completes its military withdrawal from Iraq, Baghdad declares a new era of sovereignty. But as US troops leave, questions remain over militias, foreign forces and the country's future security.

For Iraq's government in Baghdad, September 30, 2026, marks the end of an era. "October 1 will be a new day in the course of the Iraqi state, with the country free of any foreign military presence and the completion of national sovereignty over its territory," Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said in a statement.

The occasion will be celebrated as "Independence Day" with four official public holidays.

By Wednesday, the United States will have completed the withdrawal of its remaining 2,500 troops from Iraqi territory according to a 2024 agreement. Their departure concludes 12 years of the US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against the Islamic State group, or ISIS, which at the time was advancing across the country and in neighboring Syria.

The withdrawal also marks the end of more than two decades of US military involvement in Iraq. Following the US invasion in 2003, US forces withdrew in 2011 and returned in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. The withdrawal also follows the broader US strategy of reducing its military presence in the Middle East.

However, the US withdrawal does not mean an end to all foreign military deployments in Iraq.  Turkey still has troops in Iraq, even though Ankara said earlier this week that it would gradually hand over a military base in northern Iraq to Baghdad.

"In 2024, Baghdad and Washington agreed to what they called a normalized relationship," Renad Mansour, deputy director for the Middle East and North Africa program and director of the Iraq Initiative at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "For Baghdad, the political aim will be now to make clear that Iraq wants to remain an ally of the US," he said.

In his view, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is concerned that Washington could start viewing Iraq and its Iran-backed non-state militias as too close to Iran, given that the US and Israel are at war with Iran.

Baghdad extends disarmament deadline

Initially, Baghdad had linked the end of the US military mission to the disarmament of Iraq's numerous armed groups and militias. The plan also included bringing these paramilitary groups under state control.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said last week that the new deadline was June 30, 2027. The revised plan includes a 90-day period during which armed groups would refrain from attacks in exchange for assurances that US forces would not target them, followed by a gradual handover of weapons that is due to be completed by June 30, 2027.

Yet not all armed groups are likely to follow this plan as several powerful armed groups have rejected disarmament or demanded conditions that could delay the process.

"The hardest-line armed groups — Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada — have so far given no indication that they are prepared to surrender their weapons to the state and integrate into Iraq's armed forces," Alina L. Romanowski, distinguished fellow with the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council's Middle East program, said.

Renad Mansour told DW that he was not surprised by the extension of the deadline. Iraq's political landscape has been highly fragmented since the US invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein in April 2003. There have been more than eight years of war, the rise and fall of ISIS, and the US withdrawal in 2011 and return in 2014. "Many political movements are associated with armed organizations, so it is hard to see a revolution in the security sector happening any time soon," he told DW, predicting that "even next year, many armed groups will continue to remain free of the central government."

What does this mean for Iraq's minorities?

The withdrawal of US troops also includes the departure of military personnel and the removal of US air defense systems in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. Kurdish Prime Minister Masrour Barzani has already called on Baghdad for protection against missile and drone attacks from Iran. Since the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, attacks by Iraq's Iran-backed armed groups on US-linked targets in Erbil have been on the rise, while Iranian attacks on infrastructure belonging to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq have also increased.

On Monday, Kurdish officials in Erbil said that three drones targeted a camp affiliated with Iran's Kurdish opposition. Local officials said the drones were Iranian-made, but responsibility for the attack was not independently confirmed.

Yerevan Saeed, a nonresident senior fellow with the Iraq Initiative at the Atlantic Council and the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, is concerned that Iraq's vulnerable ethnic and religious minorities, such as Christians and Yazidis, as well as Kurdish communities, could be left more exposed from October 1, 2026, onward. "The withdrawal signals the end of an era in which foreign boots provided a buffer against central and regional predation," he said.

Chatham House's Mansour, meanwhile, notes that US-Iraqi ties will not end on September 30, but rather shift toward "other arenas, including economic ties rather than having a security-focused relationship."

In July, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said after meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi, that they had discussed how a sovereign, stable and strong Iraq would pave the way for mutually beneficial commercial and defense cooperation.

However, in the statement following the meeting, Hegseth added that "building a normal US-Iraq bilateral defense relationship requires a secure environment free from terrorist coercion."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Global trade weathers Iran, Ukraine and Trump's tariffs
entries.summary: Over the past six years, COVID, two wars and Donald Trump's tariffs have shaken world trade. With globalization already stalling, is this a temporary shock or the start of a great reversal?
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

Over the past six years, COVID, two wars and Donald Trump's tariffs have shaken world trade. With globalization already stalling, is this a temporary shock or the start of a great reversal?

From COVID to Donald Trump's tariffs — with wars in Ukraine and the Middle East in between — world trade policy is enduring the most unpredictable period of the postwar era.

The pandemic shut factories worldwide and accelerated a shift away from China, the world’s largest manufacturer. The two conflicts then disrupted global supplies of oil and gas, food and fertilizer.

US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, meanwhile, pushed US duties to their highest level in decades, forcing firms to find new suppliers and markets.

Robert Staiger, chief economist at the World Trade Organization (WTO), calls the turmoil "the most serious and sustained disruptions since the [world trading] system was created 80 years ago."

Goods trade buoyed by AI demand

Despite these shocks, global trade has remained surprisingly resilient.

According to the WTO's annual report published last week, goods trade volumes rose 4.6% last year, lifted by strong demand for the advanced technology behind the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. Services trade volumes grew by 5.3%.

China remained the world's largest goods exporter, while the United States was again the largest importer. The European Union came in second in both.

However, Staiger told AFP news agency last week that strong AI exports "may be masking some of the drop in world trade that might otherwise be occurring."

The WTO noted in its March trade outlook that Asian countries dominated the AI goods trade, while Africa, Latin America, the Middle East and much of Europe barely showed up.

AI-related tech accounted for about one-sixth of goods trade but close to half of global trade growth.

Washington sidesteps WTO rules

Since returning to office last year, Trump has continued to pivot from WTO rules on global trade.

The US president has set country-specific duties, breaking the WTO’s equal-treatment rule. He has since negotiated exemptions and "reciprocal" tariffs with individual countries.

Despite this, globally, about 72% of goods are still traded on the Geneva-based agency's core terms, down from roughly 80% in 2022.

On a longer horizon, though, globalization appears to have stalled. WTO data shows that since about 2015, world trade has grown only as fast as the global economy. Despite the recent geopolitical upheavals, globalization has yet to shift into reverse.

Policymakers and economists say it is too soon to know whether the wars, alongside a pivot toward protectionism in the US, China, the EU and post-Brexit Britain, mark the end of an ever-interconnected world.

"The world is certainly not becoming more globalized," Thomas Sampson, an associate professor at the London School of Economics, told DW. "But it's still an open question whether we're actually at deglobalization or just shifting around who we trade with."

How global trade is changing

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the EU has sharply cut its reliance on Russian pipeline gas from 37% in late 2021 to around 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. EU oil and coal imports from Russia are now negligible.

These moves spurred new energy deals with the US, Norway, Australia and Kazakhstan, with liquefied natural gas (LNG) replacing Russian pipeline gas.

Moscow did find new energy buyers — notably China and India — which took Russian oil at a large discount to global benchmark prices.

Camille Reverdy, an affiliate fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, doubts whether the EU will rekindle its energy trade with Moscow when the war ends.

"If the alternatives become reliable sources, I don't see it coming back," Reverdy told DW.

When the Iran war began in late February, Tehran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most critical energy transit chokepoints. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates sent some of the missing oil by pipeline to alternative ports.

According to the International Energy Agency, the world also replaced the missing millions of barrels with increased production from the US, Kazakhstan, Brazil and Venezuela. Several nations have also tapped about 300 million barrels from their strategic oil reserves, Reuters reported in August.

Almost seven months into the conflict, energy prices remain elevated, with Brent crude trading above $100 for much of the war. Several analysts are now warning of dangerously tight supply in the fall and winter.

The squeeze from Trump's tariffs is also weighing on trade.

US imports from China, for instance, fell by around 28% last year, according to the Washington-based Peterson Institute for International Economics. At the same time, its imports from the rest of the world climbed by nearly a tenth — much of it from Vietnam, Taiwan and Mexico, as part of rerouting efforts to cut reliance on Chinese suppliers.

Will Trump's strategy outlast him?

Trump’s attacks on the WTO have raised a sharper question. If the Geneva-based body were shelved, what would replace it? Experts have floated several alternatives.

These include continuing Trump's country-by-country tariffs or a web of free trade deals between economic blocs, including BRICS nations of the Global South.

The third, mooted by think tanks like Chatham House, would see the EU, Japan, Canada, Australia and Mexico keep trading by WTO-style rules at a scale the US and China could not ignore.

Bruegel's Reverdy thinks the EU would prefer a reformed WTO to the alternatives.

"The EU still wants to be seen as the leader of free and multilateral trade," she told DW, noting how Brussels has added new layers of trade policy, including possibly making Canada an associate member.

LSE's Sampson warned that continuing with Trump's "law of the jungle" would disadvantage smaller countries, who he said have a "bigger voice" under the current WTO system.

Noting how "trust in the US as a trading partner has collapsed," Sampson told DW it could take many years for confidence to return, even with a Democratic president.

WTO economists, meanwhile, have modeled different futures, noting how further trade fragmentation along geopolitical lines could cut global GDP by about 5% by 2050.

In a world in which the WTO vanished and only a patchwork of free-trade deals remained, GDP could fall closer to 7%, with the smallest and poorest economies hit hardest.

Reinforcing multilateral rules, however, could raise global GDP by roughly 3%, the agency said.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Malaysia repatriates Myanmar migrants despite UN warnings
entries.summary: Malaysia has started repatriating about 1,500 Myanmar nationals, defying warnings from the UN and rights groups. Malaysia, facing an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment, says the program is strictly voluntary.
entries.content:
Malaysia

Malaysia repatriates Myanmar migrants despite UN warnings

September 29, 2026

Malaysia has started repatriating about 1,500 Myanmar nationals, defying warnings from the UN and rights groups. Malaysia, facing an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment, says the program is strictly voluntary.

Buses accompanied by security vehicles, carrying migrants to a boat to be repatriated to Myanmar, arrived at a stadium near Malaysia's Lumut naval base on Tuesday. 

Malaysia is starting the first phase of a process agreed with Myanmar's military regime to send as many as 5,000 people back to the wartorn country.

Malaysia says the process is strictly voluntary, but the UN refugee agency and civil society organizations have voiced concerns about the security of those returning, saying they could face either military recruitment, persecution or detention amid the ongoing civil war.

What happened as Malaysia began the repatriation process?

The buses full of people arrived at the Lumuk naval base on Myanmar's northwest coast on Tuesday.

Two naval vessels and a hospital ship were docked on site seemingly ready for a naval transport.

Malaysia's Home Ministry had said in late August that the first phase of the repatriation would start in September. It said that the repatriation involved 1,476 Myanmar citizens identified by the Myanmar government.

Malaysia has tightened immigration enforcement in recent years amid rising local hostility against refugees, particularly ethnic Rohingya ⁠Muslims ​from Myanmar.

Myanmar's state media this month also cited the Foreign Ministry as saying it was working with countries to facilitate the voluntary return of verified displaced people in a safe and dignified manner.

What's the security situation in Myanmar?

Myanmar has been in more pronounced turmoil since a 2021 coup triggered a civil war, with the military now fighting armed groups across multiple frontlines.

However, allegations of persecution and even ethnic cleansing of the country's Rohingya Muslim minority were prevalent long before the full-scale civil war broke out. To the same token, some of the country's regional conflicts and uprisings have been ongoing for decades.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says the current conditions "do not suppor the safe and sustainable return of refugees from Myanmar." It also said it had not been involved in agreements like the one struck with Malaysia.

UNHCR data suggests that roughly 193,000 refugees from Myanmar are in Malaysia, around two-thirds of them Rohingya.

Activist James Bawi Thang Bik said that based on accounts of refugees who had previously been deported, they could risk detention or forced conscription.

"We fear that they may be forced to fight on the frontlines of the conflict. For many it is akin to sending them to a death sentence in their own home," he said.

A wave of online agitation this year had amplified harassment and scrutiny of Rohingya in Malaysia.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said this month that he would invite Myanmar's military chief turned president, Min Aung Hlaing, for an official visit in return for accepting the Rohingya returns.

Myanmar's largely ostracized government, trying to portray itself as more politically legitimate five years after ousting former President Aung San Suu Kyi, is seeking greater acceptance among the international community.

entries.title: AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity
entries.summary: Germany is rewriting the rules to attract data center investment from AI companies. But local communities are becoming increasingly skeptical.
entries.content:
Germany

AI: Germany plans to double data center capacity

September 29, 2026

Germany is rewriting the rules to attract data center investment from AI companies. But local communities are becoming increasingly skeptical.

The digital future is here, and it is unfolding in the town of Dietzenbach.

Google, EdgeConnex, and Maincubes, two US tech companies and one German, have each reserved a spot for a data center in the small town near Frankfurt am Main.  

Dietzenbach is a logistics hub near Frankfurt's airport, and home to 35,000 people.

The Frankfurt region, the center of Germany's financial industry, is one of the most attractive locations for digital cloud operators worldwide, and as demand for computing capacity continues to grow, more centers are planned for the region.

Locals worry about electricity and water usage

However, the news of plans for a fourth mega data center has been met with resistance by locals. The stacks of tens of thousands of computers in a data center need a high supply of energy to run around the clock. They radiate large amounts of heat and need cooling, which requires huge quantities of water.

The people of Dietzenbach DW met were worried about their water and electricity bills rising, as well as a higher temperature in their town.

"We want to know two things: What are the benefits for the local community here in Dietzenbach? And what are the environmental impacts?" said Dietzenbach resident Wilhelm Sauer, pointing at the four imposing chimneys rising from the EdgeConnex data center.

He and the other local activists believe that the toll the data centers will take on regional resources may not be offset by the limited number of new jobs announced.

Dietzenbach's mayor, Dieter Lang of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, is optimistic. He predicted that around 100 "high-value jobs" would come to his town through the Google data center. 

He also expects it will benefit his city's coffers: "We expect a substantial tax contribution," Lang told DW.

But Tara Merk, researcher on Community Data Centers at the Weizenbaum Institute, is skeptical: She believes Germany can probably expect little revenue from data centers operated by US companies, "because the profits may be taxed elsewhere."

"Especially thinking about big tech companies — they're not going to be doing their taxes in Dietzenbach," she told DW.

Data centers and lack of information

In August 2026, the German government launched a data centers registry listing energy consumption, water consumption, and energy efficiency measures for the data centers that are already operating.  

But the list includes only around 300 data centers, far fewer than the estimated 2,000 data centers the government says are running across the country.

"Some companies report their smaller projects but not the big ones," Werner Neumann, board member of the environmental group BUND, told DW.

There is no official overview of how many data centers are being built or where. The civil society project Heisse Luft (Hot Air) has decided to fill these information gap, and has developed an online map of the planned data centers across Germany. The map is updated every day with information based on crowdsourcing from local communities.  

"Theoretically, we should have access to this information," Tiziana von Witzleben, co-founder of the Heisse Luft initiative, told DW. "Maybe the German government doesn't have the capacity to [collect this information] and share it. But I believe it is on purpose, particularly [on the part of] big players like Google and Amazon. [They] are known to be very secretive about what they do. Because they know that if they tell people, they will get a lot of protest."

Unlike in the US, where a nationwide movement mobilized protests all over the country, protests against data centers in Germany remain a local community phenomenon.  

In February, the local council of Groß-Gerau in the Frankfurt region voted against a €2.5-billion ($2.8-billion) data center proposed by a US operator, at least partly as a result of massive protests from the residents wary of heat waste, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.

In Maintal, another town in the region, an EdgeConnex mega data center faced intense protest against its plans to build its own gas-fired power plant. The €1-billion project is now searching for power alternatives in a region which is already hitting its grid limits.

The race for computational power

Germany is the largest data center market in Europe, both by capacity and number of sites, and the Frankfurt/Rhine-Main region, which includes Dietzenbach, holds over a third of the country's total data center capacity.

Its proximity to the Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX) infrastructure in Frankfurt makes the region attractive for digital cloud operators.

To achieve its strategic goal of doubling data center capacity by 2030, the federal government, a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the SPD, has proposed amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) that regulates energy consumption and climate protection.  

The environmentalist Green Party questions whether the targets are based on real demand. The socialist Left Party, on the other hand, is skeptical of the expansion as a whole. Both parties oppose the government's plans to relax the rules to attract more data centers.  

On the opposite end of the political spectrum, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) supports the expansion of data centers but criticizes the law promoting the use of renewable energy to power them.  

Why are energy efficiency amendments controversial?

The proposed amendment would push back the deadline for operators to achieve renewable energy targets, and would relax requirements for the reuse of heat waste.

Despite this plan, Tara Merk still considers the push for energy-efficient data centers in Germany to be a progressive example in the global context.  

But she is critical of the parts of the law that would give companies the right to declare that the data on the amount of water and electricity they use are trade secrets.

"This proposed amendment shifts the regulatory landscape very much in favor of operators," she told DW. "Having good data is needed to regulate, intervene, and build trust and acceptance within local communities."

"I think [lack of transparency] is ultimately going to foster more antagonism between data centers and local communities, making it harder for operators to expand or even keep their existing sites running the way they are," Merk warned.

Algorithm Watch, an AI watchdog, argued in a public statement that the legal changes the government is proposing are not about cutting bureaucracy, but more about appeasing US tech giants Microsoft, Google, and Vantage.   

"German and European operators mostly have no problem with the current rules," Algorithm Watch said. "The amendments run counter to the government's own aim of strengthening German/European firms."

This summer, the watchdog launched a campaign and collected 150,000 signatures against the amendments to the law, calling for the public reporting obligations of data centers to be retained.

The amendments were presented to the Bundestag in September. If the new law passes, the government hopes it will take effect in January.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: Spain grows fruit and vegetables for Europe — but it's running out of water
entries.summary: Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.

Donana National Park in southwestern Spain — one of Europe's most important wetlands, home to millions of migratory birds and threatened species like the Iberian lynx — is running dry. But rising temperatures and drought caused by climate change are only part of the problem.

The UNESCO-protected region on the Atlantic coast relies on an underground aquifer that's been tapped by hundreds of illegal wells. The reason: Europe's fruit and vegetable supply. Spain provides one-quarter of Europe's fresh produce, supplying colder parts of the continent with fruit and vegetables year-round.

The scale of water extraction in Spain is staggering: In 2016, WWF Spain estimated that the Donana wetland was home to over 1,000 illegal wells and more than 1,700 ponds illegally irrigating an area as big as 4,200 football fields.

"It's gotten hotter every year. And the water dries up so quickly," one local resident in the town of El Rocio, just north of the wetlands, told DW.

"For me, day to day, the main issue is my animals," said another, hitching his horse up to a tourist carriage. "I have to draw water for them, but the well doesn't have enough water to provide it all at once."

Strawberries are lucrative — but come with a cost

The Donana area used to be royal hunting grounds, consisting of marshes and ponds. In the early 20th century, parts began to be used for dryland farming, agriculture in arid regions that relies heavily on rainwater.

But in 1971, Spain — still under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco — declared the region's irrigation to be of national interest. The Almonte-Marismas Plan, named after the aquifer it tapped into, was part of a massive, state-sponsored effort to increase food production.

Authorities decided to bet on strawberries, which they called "red gold." According to calculations based on FAO data, strawberries can yield up to €150,000 (about $170,000) in gross revenue per hectare per year, compared to roughly €20,000 for potatoes or €15,000 for grapes.

But growing strawberries at scale also meant using a lot more water. Authorities handed out generous quotas and allotments, seemingly without considering how much extraction the aquifer could handle. Even those legal quotas weren't enough for the ever-expanding fields.

Farmers turned to illegal wells and reservoirs to make up the difference. They built them to stockpile water, draining supplies from local residents and the UNESCO World Heritage Site next door.

"There was extreme drought and lack of attention from the administration," said Pedro Banez, of the Condado Water Users' Association. "And we found ourselves with a number of farms — or parts of farms — that fell outside the land classified as irrigable agricultural land."

Police, NGOs track down water thieves

The turning point came in 2019 when, following numerous reports of unlawful wells, a 2-year-old fell into deep, reportedly illegal borehole on farmland near Malaga and died. In the aftermath, Spain's Civil Guard police force created dedicated units focused on water theft.

Two years after that, in 2021, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Spain had failed to protect the Donana aquifer, finding the country in violation of EU law.

Today, police and NGOs like WWF Spain track illegal extraction — near Donana, and other overtaxed agricultural regions across the country — using a mix of old and new tools. They start with satellite images of the region, comparing them against land rights maps to flag areas that appear greener than their legal status allows. Drones follow, giving investigators a closer look at where the water is actually coming from.

Some wells are completely illegal. Others are legal but extract more than they're allowed, which requires closer, on-site inspection to prove.

Investigators check the flow meters that measure how much water a well is pulling. Tampering is common, often using a powerful magnet which disrupts the internal mechanism of the flow meter, allowing water to pass through unrecorded.

Farmers caught extracting illegally can be charged with crimes against the environment and fraud. Most face fines, but sentences can run up to five years in prison.

Spain's government, farmers tackle water misuse

In a bid to undo decades of overuse, local and national authorities have negotiated a €1.4 billion joint plan. The government has continued shutting down illegal wells, sealing almost 300 in the Donana region alone.

Officials have also started buying up farmland, rewilding it and turning it into protected areas, while setting up funds to create jobs in other sectors like tourism and renewable energy.

Farmers, meanwhile, have had to change how they water their crops.

Many have switched to drip irrigation systems, where each plant gets its own individual dripper, paired with moisture sensors that report exactly how much water a plant needs. That cuts down on the overuse of both water and fertilizer.

Farmers have also begun planting less water-intensive crops and shifting their growing season to colder months.

Sustainable solutions to secure water

Spain isn't alone in confronting this problem. As economies mature, fruit and vegetable production starts being outsourced to places with cheaper labor, fewer restrictions and more sun.

Mexico, Brazil and Colombia grow food for parts of the US, while countries in southeast Asia export a lot of produce to China or Japan. Some countries in northern Africa, including Morocco and Egypt, also supply fresh fruits and vegetables to their European neighbors to the north. But, as in Spain, intensive agriculture has strained local water supplies.

Morocco has tried to turn the tide by using satellite comparisons to monitor irrigation and offering subsidies for farmers who switch to drip irrigation. In India, the government is trying to move farmers toward less water-intensive crops.

And in California, the US state has paid farmers to halt certain types of irrigation and introduced legislation to monitor and allocate water more sustainably.

Securing water, no longer seen as an unlimited resource, will increasingly be a challenge as the effects of climate change intensify. Addressing overextraction will take a coordinated effort from governments, farmers and the industries that depend on their water.

Additional research by Nicole Ris.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler, Sarah Steffen

entries.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
entries.summary: A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.
entries.content:
Argentina

Argentina threatens UK legal action over Falklands oil

September 29, 2026

A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.

The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.

What has Argentina threatened to do?

Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.

"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.

Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.

His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.

Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.

What is the Sea Lion oil project?

Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.

The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.

Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.

The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.

Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?

The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.

Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.

The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.

The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.

In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.

Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
